title: Knowledge Check 10 - Lessons 46-50
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 46-50 - Testing, Deployment, and Maintenance. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: Which set of cases gives the most useful test of an agent that is already live?
options: Cases generated only from subagent metadata, because they match the configuration
One long conversation that walks through every subagent in order
Utterances pulled from real sessions in Agent Analytics and Session Trace, including typos, topic changes, and half-formed requests
Cases written by the product owner from the requirements document
questions.explanation: Real session utterances carry the phrasing customers actually use, which is where routing and response failures show up, while tidy generated or authored cases test the agent you designed.

questions.question: An action assertion passes for a conversation-level test. What did it actually verify?
options: That every expected action occurred, even though the agent may also have performed extra actions
That the agent performed exactly the expected actions and nothing else
That the underlying records were updated correctly
That the actions ran under the running user's permissions
questions.explanation: The conversation-level action rule is that the test passes when all expected actions occurred, so extra actions do not fail it and record updates are not checked.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks whether a passing response quality score proves the agent's reply was correct. What is the honest answer?
options: Yes, because the judge compares the reply to ground truth in the CRM
Yes, provided the suite ran on Live Data
No, because the response evaluation is only an assertion
No, because the score is a judge model comparing the reply to the expected response you wrote, so a vague expected response produces a confident but inaccurate score
questions.explanation: The judge scores against your expected response rather than against verified truth, which is why the quality of that expected text decides whether the number means anything.

questions.question: Which evaluations run automatically on every agent test, before you add any quality evaluation?
options: Completeness, coherence, and conciseness
Latency and instruction adherence
Only the custom scorers you define
Response evaluation, subagent assertion, and action assertion
questions.explanation: The default tier is response evaluation, subagent assertion, and action assertion, while the quality scorers are opt-in additions.

questions.question: A conversation-level test expects a lookup and an email. The agent performs the lookup, sends the email, and creates an extra case. What is the result, and why?
options: Fail, because the agent performed an action that was not expected
Pass, because every expected action occurred even though the agent also performed an additional action
Fail, because the action assertion compares the exact action sequence
Pass, because the response evaluation overrides the action assertion
questions.explanation: The conversation-level action assertion passes when all expected actions occurred and is not failed by extra actions, so the additional case does not break the test.

questions.question: Which scorer reports a value of HIGH, LOW, or UNCERTAIN rather than a pass, a fail, or a number?
options: Completeness
Latency
Instruction adherence
Subagent assertion
questions.explanation: Instruction adherence is the scorer that reports HIGH, LOW, or UNCERTAIN, while the assertions report pass or fail and latency reports milliseconds.

questions.question: A case passes the subagent assertion and the action assertion, but its response quality score is low. What does that combination tell you?
options: The agent routed and acted as expected and phrased the answer badly, so the fix belongs in the subagent instructions or the prompt
The agent routed the utterance to the wrong subagent
The expected response field was left empty
Latency is the root cause of the low score
questions.explanation: Passing assertions with low quality scores means routing and action selection were correct and the wording was the problem, which points at the instructions rather than at classification.

questions.question: Your release suite passed on the current agent version. You change one subagent instruction, rerun the same suite, and three cases now fail. What is the correct next step?
options: Delete the failing cases so the suite is green again
Update the test set to match the new agent behavior
Read the failing cells for the judge's reasoning and the JSON output, then retest those utterances in Agentforce Builder to confirm the break before adjusting the instruction
Rerun the suite until the failures stop appearing
questions.explanation: A case that moved from pass to fail is a regression signal, and the vendor's remedy is to read the detail panel and retest the utterance manually in Builder before changing the agent again.

questions.question: A colleague argues a run is good because every assertion passed. What is the correction?
options: Assertions cover response quality as well as routing
Assertions confirm only that the expected subagent and actions were selected, so a case can pass both and still score low on response quality
Assertions are scored by the judge model, so they already include quality
Assertions fail whenever the agent performs extra actions
questions.explanation: Assertions answer the routing and action question only, so a fully green assertion column says nothing about how good the replies were, and extra actions never fail the action assertion.

questions.question: An admin must move an agent with three versions from a v68 sandbox to a v68 production org and confirm every version plus the correct action versions travel. Which approach does this?
options: Deploy AiAgentDefinition alone and let each action resolve itself at run time
Retrieve with AiAgentDefinitionVersion using MyAgent#* and deploy with the root-type-with-dependencies flag set to AiAgentDefinitionVersion
Copy the agent by exporting a CSV of the Testing Center cases and importing it in production
Recreate the agent by hand in production and skip the metadata deploy
questions.explanation: The hash star retrieves every version and the root-type-with-dependencies flag pulls the correct version of each flow, Apex, and prompt template action, which is exactly what a multi-version move needs.

questions.question: After a clean metadata deploy, the agent exists in production but nobody can use it and its Flow action does not run. Which missing step best explains both symptoms?
options: The manifest omitted the AiAgentDefinition top-level definition
The production org is on an older API version than the sandbox
The agent was built with Agent Script but the AiAuthoringBundle was left out
The agent was never activated and the agent user was never assigned the permissions its actions need
questions.explanation: Deployment makes the agent exist and activation makes it operational, and an action runs under the agent user, so an unactivated agent or an unpermissioned user produces an agent that is present and unusable.

questions.question: An agent that reads a custom contact field works in the sandbox but its action fails at run time only in production. What is the most likely cause?
options: The agent user in production lacks field-level view permission on the custom contact field
The custom contact field cannot be referenced by any agent action
The agent metadata type does not support custom fields
The sandbox and production have different agent versions, which breaks actions regardless of permissions
questions.explanation: Actions run under the running user, and the agent user must have permission on everything the agent touches, so missing field-level access on the custom field fails the action only where that user lacks it.

questions.question: An agent's action that queries records succeeds in the sandbox but throws an access error only in production. Which cause fits the evidence best?
options: The agent metadata type does not support query actions
The flow that backs the action was deployed but left on an inactive version in both orgs
The agent user in production lacks the object, field, or sharing access the action needs
The agent was built in the legacy builder and cannot run in production
questions.explanation: Actions run under the running user, so an access error isolated to production points to the agent user's permissions or sharing access there, which a Testing Center run in the sandbox would not reveal.

questions.question: A service agent is active and answering in the builder, but customers cannot reach it from the company website. Which step was most likely missed?
options: Publish the Embedded Service Deployment for the channel in the target org
Retrieve the agent metadata a second time
Re-create the agent user with a new username
Deploy the agent a second time with the root-type-with-dependencies flag removed
questions.explanation: Channel plumbing such as Embedded Service Deployments is separate from the agent metadata, so an agent that is active but unreachable is usually missing the channel step and the web deployment publish.

questions.question: Which of these pieces of an agent setup is re-established in production rather than migrated, and is the reason an agent can work in the sandbox and fail after go-live?
options: The subagent instructions
The default system messages
The variables and filters defined on the template
Authentication to an external data vendor connection, which is per org
questions.explanation: External connections and their authentication are scoped to the org, so they do not travel with the agent and must be re-established in production, unlike the portable definitions such as instructions, messages, variables, and filters.
